title: Asset and Cover
premise: Paloma Pemberton, a disgraced intelligence analyst fired from three agencies for asking the wrong questions, is pulled back in when a dead colleague's voiceprint unlocks a server in Lisbon containing proof that a planned defector extraction is actually a trap designed to eliminate a witness to an allied minister's crimes. As she races to extract the defector, Elena Vasquez, before the Geneva summit convenes, Paloma discovers her own family's inheritance is entangled with the conspiracy—her late father helped build it. Betrayed by her handler and hunted by both services, she must choose between burning the truth publicly or trading it for her survival. In the end, she gets Elena out alive but releases the evidence herself at the summit's edge, sacrificing her anonymity and inheriting not wealth, but responsibility.
about_author: Ines Joubert is a former compliance auditor who spent a decade inside multinational banks before turning to fiction full-time. She writes from a farmhouse in the Dordogne, drawing on her obsession with paperwork as the true architecture of power.

chapters.title: The Rules of Disappearance
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. Twelve years after her third firing, she lives quietly in Marseille doing freelance risk assessments, rigidly invisible. A package arrives containing a dead colleague's old burner phone. The emotional beat is dread: the past has found her, and she knows invisibility was always rented, never owned.

chapters.title: Voiceprint
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. The phone plays a recorded phrase in her former mentor Aldous Wren's voice; when she speaks the counterphrase aloud, it unlocks a remote server in Lisbon. She finds fragmented files on 'Operation Glasshouse'—a defector extraction scheduled before the Geneva summit. Beat: reluctant curiosity curdling into alarm.

chapters.title: Three Agencies, Three Funerals
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV, with flashback texture. She investigates why Wren died—officially a heart attack—and maps how each of her firings coincided with her touching Glasshouse-adjacent material. The beat is bitter clarity: her career wasn't ruined by incompetence; it was pruned deliberately.

chapters.title: The Minister's Ledger
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. Decrypted files implicate British Home Office minister Charles Redgrave in laundering cartel money through a charity tied to Paloma's father's estate. Beat: vertigo—the conspiracy isn't just professional; it runs through her own bloodline and inheritance.

chapters.title: Contact
chapters.summary: Elena Vasquez's POV, introduced in Lisbon safehouse. Elena, the defector, suspects she's bait but walks into the network anyway because her daughter is being held as leverage. Beat: cold pragmatism masking terror; she trusts no one, least of all whoever comes to extract her.

chapters.title: Handler
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. Her old handler, Marcus Ives, resurfaces offering official sanction if she delivers Elena quietly before the summit. Paloma smells the trap but accepts, needing resources and access. Beat: self-aware complicity—she's choosing to be used, calculating she can turn the use around.

chapters.title: Lisbon Tiles
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. Surveillance tradecraft through Alfama: she confirms Elena is real, alive, and watched by at least three separate teams—including one that doesn't answer to any service she recognizes. Beat: rising tension; the trap has more layers than the files suggested.

chapters.title: What the Father Built
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV, interleaved with her father's letters. She excavates the family trust and finds his old consultancy seeded the laundering structure Redgrave now uses. Beat: grief weaponized—she stops mourning her father and starts interrogating him, deciding the inheritance must be spent, not preserved.

chapters.title: First Contact
chapters.summary: Alternating Paloma/Elena POVs. Their first meeting in a tram tunnel: mutual interrogation, knife-edge distrust. Elena tests Paloma with a false detail; Paloma catches it. Beat: grudging recognition—two women who survive by assuming betrayal, cautiously aligning.

chapters.title: Ives Reports
chapters.summary: Marcus Ives's POV. He briefs his true principal—not the agency, but Redgrave's fixer—confirming Paloma has located Elena. He argues for letting the extraction proceed so both women can be erased abroad. Beat: banal corruption; Ives tells himself he's protecting institutions, not committing murder.

chapters.title: The Daughter
chapters.summary: Elena's POV. Elena discovers her daughter has been moved to a facility outside Porto, confirming the leverage is live and time-bound to the summit. She gives Paloma an ultimatum: child first, testimony second. Beat: maternal ferocity overriding spycraft logic.

chapters.title: Glasshouse Protocol
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. She decodes the full protocol: the 'extraction' is designed to fail publicly, discrediting defector testimony before the summit. Every route out of Lisbon is pre-sealed. Beat: claustrophobic realization that the plan's elegance is its horror.

chapters.title: Safehouse Fire
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. The Lisbon safehouse burns with two of her contracted support staff inside—an unmistakable message. Paloma realizes Ives sold her location. Beat: rage transmuted into resolve; the price of survival is now counted in other people's blood.

chapters.title: Porto Run
chapters.summary: Paloma and Elena's alternating POVs. A night drive north to reach Elena's daughter, dodging a tail that splits into two cars. They get the girl out through a school gala cover. Beat: adrenaline and fragile trust hardening into partnership under fire.

chapters.title: The Bait Confirmed
chapters.summary: Elena's POV. Elena reveals she's known since week one that she was bait—but the server data Wren left includes names of eleven other witnesses already disappeared. Her testimony isn't optional; silence equals their erasure. Beat: moral weight settling on both women.

chapters.title: Geneva Bound
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. Train from Porto toward Geneva with forged credentials; Ives boards the same train. A quiet carriage confrontation where he offers Paloma her old life back if she hands over Elena and the ledger. Beat: temptation articulated perfectly—and refused.

chapters.title: Derailment
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. Ives triggers a stop; armed contractors sweep the train. Paloma splits from Elena, drawing pursuit through freight yards, wounded but mobile. Beat: sacrifice and competence—Paloma finally uses everything that got her fired, on her own terms.

chapters.title: Summit Eve
chapters.summary: Elena's POV. Elena and her daughter reach Geneva separately, sheltered by a journalist ally of Wren's. Elena prepares her testimony while learning Redgrave will chair the very session meant to hear defectors. Beat: dark irony sharpening to a point.

chapters.title: The Ledger Goes Public
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. Rather than trade the evidence for safety, Paloma pushes the full Glasshouse archive—her father's structure included—to press rooms and delegates simultaneously. Beat: cathartic self-immolation; she burns her own name alongside the guilty.

chapters.title: Redgrave's Room
chapters.summary: Climax, Paloma's POV. Confrontation in a summit annex: Redgrave offers inheritance, absolution, even truth-as-managed-release. Paloma refuses; Ives, exposed, wavers; security arrives tipped by the journalist. Beat: power meeting its match in a woman with nothing left to lose.

chapters.title: Testimony
chapters.summary: Elena's POV. Elena testifies before an emergency panel as Redgrave resigns mid-session; arrests ripple outward. Paloma watches from the gallery, anonymous by choice for the last time. Beat: justice rendered imperfectly but undeniably; grief for Wren and her father finally allowed.

chapters.title: Asset No Longer
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV, epilogue. Months later, Paloma declines three job offers and instead funds a small foundation from the liquidated family trust to protect whistleblowers' families. Elena sends a postcard from somewhere warm. Beat: earned peace—the price of survival paid, and worth it.
